About me

Welcome!

I’m a Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation Postdoctoral Fellow and a UW Data Science Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Washington, working with David Shean in the Terrain Analysis and Cryosphere Observation (TACO) Lab.

I earned my Ph.D. in Civil and Environmental Engineering at UW in 2025. My dissertation focused on improving measurements of surface movement and snow depth in mountain environments using synthetic aperture radar. I received my B.A. in Geology and Biology from Middlebury College in 2020.

This site brings together my academic work and my interests in cartography and taking pictures of mountains.

Research

My research uses remote sensing and data science to understand mountain hazards and water resources. I investigate how slopes move before failure, how buried ice shapes the evolution of moraines damming glacial lakes, and how snow is distributed across the western United States. By developing methods that take advantage of the vast quantity of satellite data, I work towards the detailed understanding of mountain processes needed to inform hazard assessment and water resource management.

01 / Landslides

Identifying and monitoring unstable mountain slopes

I use satellite and airborne radar interferometry (InSAR) and feature tracking to identify unstable mountain slopes and precisely quantify their movement over time. My work spans the western United States, Alaska, Patagonia, and High Mountain Asia, including investigations of movement preceding major slope failures. I’m working toward automated monitoring systems that combine large-scale satellite observations and AI to identify landslides that warrant close attention, track their behavior, and provide timely information for hazard assessment.

02 / Glacial lake outburst floods

Assessing unstable dams and reconstructing past floods

I investigate glacial lake outburst flood hazards across High Mountain Asia, including high-priority sites in Nepal, India, and China. I use satellite InSAR and feature tracking to quantify moraine dam movement and subsidence, and developed an approach using seasonal changes in InSAR coherence to map buried ice within these dams. I also use coherence change to map the impacts of past floods and debris flows, and to constrain when historical floods occurred. Together, this work informs glacial lake outburst flood hazard assessment and improves our understanding of processes controlling moraine dam evolution.

03 / Snow

Mapping mountain snow with machine learning

I develop machine learning models to map snow depth across the western United States, capturing local snow patterns across entire mountain ranges. Trained on high-resolution airborne lidar measurements, these models combine remote sensing observations with model-based inputs to estimate snow depth at 50 m resolution. I’ve released open-source software that makes these estimates available for any location in the western U.S. and any date over roughly the past decade. This work supports efforts to quantify the water stored in mountain snow and track its distribution through the season.

The map at the top of this page uses deep-snow to predict snow depth across the North Cascades. It is generated daily from remote sensing data.

04 / Rock glaciers

Rock glacier motion and mountain hydrology

I use airborne and satellite InSAR to investigate rock glacier motion across the western United States. I developed a kinematic inventory of rock glaciers in Utah to characterize their movement and examine where they form and persist. I’m particularly interested in using surface motion to infer their internal properties and thickness. My ongoing work explores how rock glaciers evolve over time and their roles in shaping alpine landscapes and storing and releasing water.

Teaching &
mentorship

I want students to develop an understanding of natural processes through experimentation. My teaching combines discussion, interactive coding, and field-based learning. Jupyter notebooks let students connect equations, code, maps, and observations while building scientific computing skills.

I also emphasize writing and presentation as part of doing science. In teaching and mentorship, I value clear expectations, open communication, and practical support for students with different backgrounds and levels of experience.

2026 / University of Washington

Geospatial Data Analysis

Instructor of record for a combined graduate and undergraduate course with 19 students. Previously a teaching assistant in 2024 and 2025, and a contributor to course development.

2026 / Juneau Icefield Research Program

Research in the field

Led a research project with eight undergraduates evaluating the first NISAR glacier velocity measurements of the Juneau Icefield; taught remote sensing lectures to 31 students and led small-group technical workshops.

Mentorship & workshops

Learning through research and software

I have led GitHub Actions tutorials at SciPy and US-RSE and projects at NASA Earth Sciences / UW and GeoSmart hackweeks.
